dictionary.item: an AI agent that designs the OpenAPI schema
an AI agent that interviews the user, asking for project details. Its role is to be the primary point of contact with the user.
an AI agent responsible for designing the database, ensuring it follows normal forms.

At this stage, the softest possible schema check. Allow common constructs that are used everywhere. This is a minimal but sufficient set of OpenAPI (3.x) fields for an early stage — excluding anything that can be added later.
## Root level
- **openapi** — spec version (e.g. `3.0.3` or `3.1.0`) - **info** — `title`, `version`, `description` (a brief summary of the API) - **servers** — at least one base URL (a placeholder like `http://localhost:3000` is fine) - **paths** — the endpoints themselves
## For each path/operation
- **summary** — one line describing what the endpoint does - **operationId** — useful for code generation and for agents/tooling that parse the spec - **parameters** — if there are path/query parameters: `name`, `in`, `required`, `schema` - **requestBody** — for POST/PUT/PATCH: `content` → `application/json` → `schema` - **responses** — at least one success code (200/201) and one error code (400 or a general 4xx), with `description` and `content.application/json.schema`
## Schemas (components/schemas)
- Extract repeated objects into `components/schemas` and reference them via `$ref` - For each schema: `type`, `properties` (with `type` for each field), `required` — this is enough at this stage, no need for `format`, `example`, `pattern`, or other refinements yet
## What can safely be deferred
- `examples` / `example` (except when the API is unclear without them) - `security` / `securitySchemes` (if auth hasn't been settled yet) - `tags`, detailed `description` on every field - `default`, `enum` bounds, `minLength`/`maximum`, and other validation details - `deprecated`, `externalDocs` - multiple `servers` for different environments - `oneOf`/`anyOf`/`allOf` — adds complexity to reading; add these once real polymorphism actually appears
**Rule of thumb:** if a field doesn't affect "how to call the endpoint and what you get back," it can be deferred. Everything in the first block above typically covers 90% of the practical value a spec needs at the start (frontend can generate a client, QA can write tests, an agent/LLM can understand the contract).

task.task-body:
Right now the backender AI agent produces a schema, but we don't validate it. There's no guarantee it won't turn out invalid and break the frontend application downstream. The problem runs deeper — this would mean violating the principle of documentation accuracy and trustworthiness that the platform is built on. The way out is to follow a two-pronged strategy.
The OpenAPI schema is valid — no syntax errors
The OpenAPI schema follows the rules and constraints we enforce at the platform level
Only these two conditions together guarantee the schema is valid and safe to pass further down the pipeline.
